summary: Climb to a tomb hidden in a cleft of the cliff, where the gods of the night are drawn like stick figures on a giant papyrus unrolled around the walls.
look: High in a narrow cleft at the far end of the valley, reached by steep metal stairs, then a steep corridor that crosses a deep well shaft on a bridge. Beyond it are the antechamber, lined with rows of tiny gods, and the oval, cartouche-shaped burial chamber with the red quartzite sarcophagus. Expect heat and stooping.
story:
Thutmose III reigned 54 years, the first two decades alongside his aunt and stepmother Hatshepsut. Then he fought at least 16 campaigns, beginning with the victory at Megiddo in his 23rd year, which is why the American Egyptologist James Breasted called him the Napoleon of Egypt.

His tomb is cut high in the cliff of the furthest wadi, a deliberate hiding place. The corridor bends in a dog-leg and drops past a deep well, designed to stop robbers. It did not work: the tomb was plundered in antiquity and its location forgotten until Victor Loret found it in 1898.

The decoration is unlike almost anything else in the valley. On a yellowish background meant to look like aged papyrus, the Amduat is drawn in black and red outline, its deities as quick, almost naive stick figures, the text in the cursive hand of sacred books. The antechamber lists the 741 gods and demons of the Amduat. The burial chamber is shaped like a cartouche, the first of its kind. On a pillar, the king is suckled by Isis in the form of a tree. The red quartzite sarcophagus is cartouche-shaped too.

The king was not inside. His mummy was found in the Deir el-Bahari cache in 1881 and is now at NMEC.
details: Antechamber walls: rows of tiny figures, a catalogue of the 741 deities of the Amduat.
Burial chamber walls: the Amduat in black and red on yellow, like a papyrus unrolled around the room.
A pillar in the burial chamber: a tree reaching out an arm and a breast to feed the king. The tree is Isis.
The red quartzite sarcophagus, shaped like a cartouche, still in place.
The ceiling: yellow stars on blue over the burial chamber.
fun_fact: Thutmose's own mother was a minor queen called Isis, so the tree goddess Isis nursing him on the pillar is a neat double meaning.
narration: You have climbed to the tomb of Thutmose the Third, the great conqueror of the 18th Dynasty. For his first 20 years his aunt Hatshepsut ruled beside him. Then he fought at least 16 campaigns, from Syria to Nubia, and an American Egyptologist later called him the Napoleon of Egypt. His tomb was hidden as well as possible: high in a cleft of the cliff, then down a steep corridor and across a deep well shaft meant to stop thieves. It failed. The tomb was robbed in antiquity, and his mummy turned up in the priests' hiding place at Deir el-Bahari. Now look at the walls. This is the Amduat, the book of what is in the underworld, drawn in black and red on a yellowish background, like a giant papyrus unrolled around the room. The hundreds of gods are quick, simple figures, almost cartoons. The burial chamber itself is shaped like a cartouche, the oval ring drawn around a royal name, so the king lies inside his own name. Find the pillar where a tree reaches out an arm and a breast to feed the king: that tree is the goddess Isis.

summary: Victor Loret found a king still in his sarcophagus here, and side rooms full of hidden royal mummies, including Tutankhamun's grandmother and mother.
look: A steep descent: stairs and corridors drop past a deep well shaft into a pillared hall and a large rectangular burial chamber, with an upper level of pillars and a lower crypt holding the cartouche-shaped sarcophagus. Only the burial chamber is decorated: the Amduat on the walls, and on the pillars the king before the gods.
story:
On 9 March 1898 the French Egyptologist Victor Loret entered this tomb and found something no one had seen in the valley: a king still in his own sarcophagus. Amenhotep II, son of Thutmose III, was a famous athlete; a stela he set up by the Sphinx boasts of his rowing and of arrows shot through copper targets.

Then Loret opened the side rooms. Priests of the Third Intermediate Period had hidden a second royal cache here, identified by labels on the wrappings: Thutmose IV, Amenhotep III, Merenptah, Seti II, Siptah, Ramesses IV, V and VI. In another room lay three unwrapped bodies side by side: an older woman, a younger woman and a boy. DNA studies published in 2010 identified the 'Elder Lady' as Queen Tiye, wife of Amenhotep III, and showed that the 'Younger Lady' was a daughter of Amenhotep III and Tiye and the mother of Tutankhamun. Her name is still unknown. Another unidentified woman lay in an upturned coffin lid inscribed for Setnakht.

The tomb has the classic early 18th Dynasty dog-leg plan. Its decoration is in the same papyrus style as Thutmose III's. The kings' mummies, and the Elder Lady, are now at NMEC, moved there in the Pharaohs' Golden Parade of 2021.
details: Burial chamber pillars: Amenhotep II face to face with Osiris, Anubis and Hathor.
The sarcophagus in the lower crypt: where Loret found the king still lying in 1898.
Burial chamber walls: the Amduat on yellow, drawn like a papyrus, as in Thutmose III's tomb.
The small side rooms off the burial chamber: in two of them the cached kings and the three unwrapped bodies were found.
fun_fact: The 'Younger Lady' was Tutankhamun's mother and, DNA suggests, also his father's sister. Royal family trees in Egypt could be very short.
narration: Amenhotep the Second, son of Thutmose the Third, was buried here, and he was a royal show-off: on a stela near the Sphinx he boasts of rowing better than his sailors and shooting arrows through copper targets. In March 1898 the French archaeologist Victor Loret came down here by candlelight and found something unique: a king still lying in his own sarcophagus. Then he opened the side rooms and found more kings. Around 3,000 years ago, priests had hidden other royal mummies here to save them from robbers: Thutmose the Fourth, Amenhotep the Third, Merenptah and several Ramesses among them. In another room lay three bodies side by side, an older woman, a younger woman and a boy. DNA tests published in 2010 showed that the older woman was Queen Tiye, Tutankhamun's grandmother, and that the younger one was Tutankhamun's mother. We still do not know her name. The kings are now in Cairo. In the burial chamber, look at the pillars, where the king stands face to face with Osiris, Anubis and Hathor.

summary: Howard Carter's first royal tomb, found 19 years before Tutankhamun, with an ancient note recording that the king's burial was repaired after robbers.
look: A dog-leg tomb: corridors down to a deep well shaft, a pillared hall where the axis turns 90 degrees, then the burial chamber with a huge red stone sarcophagus. Only the well room and the antechamber are painted, with the king before the gods under ceilings of yellow stars on blue.
story: Howard Carter found this tomb in January 1903 while working for the American millionaire Theodore Davis. Thutmose IV is the king of the Dream Stele between the Sphinx's paws, which you saw at Giza on the 12th. Robbers had been here first, but they left a chariot body once covered in silver leaf, a leather archer's gauntlet, and in a side room the mummy of a young boy, probably Prince Amenemhat. The king himself had been moved to the cache in Amenhotep II's tomb. The red sarcophagus has Nephthys at the head and Isis at the feet. On the right-hand wall of the antechamber, an ink inscription of year 8 of Horemheb records that the treasurer Maya was ordered to renew the burial of Thutmose IV; his assistant Djehutymose added a line.
details: Right-hand wall of the antechamber: the ink note of year 8 of Horemheb about restoring the burial.
Well room, left wall: Thutmose before Osiris, Anubis and Hathor.
The red sarcophagus: Nephthys at the head end, Isis at the feet, texts filled in yellow.
fun_fact: The Dream Stele says a sleeping prince was promised the throne by the Sphinx if he cleared away its sand. This tomb is what he got for his trouble.
narration: Here lay Thutmose the Fourth, the prince who, according to the Dream Stele between the paws of the Sphinx, was promised the throne if he cleared away the sand. In January 1903 Howard Carter found it, nineteen years before Tutankhamun. Thieves had beaten him to it, but they left a chariot, an archer's leather glove and a huge red sarcophagus. Less than a century after the burial, the state stepped in. On the right-hand wall of the antechamber, a note in ink, dated to year 8 of King Horemheb, records that the treasurer Maya was ordered to restore this king's burial. Find that faint line of black writing: it is one of the earliest records of an official reburial.

summary: The tomb of a teenage king with a deformed foot, a figurehead for a queen and a foreign chancellor, whose name was cut out and carved back in.
look: In the southern part of the valley, a long tomb whose first corridors are finely carved and painted with the Litany of Ra, vultures spreading their wings across the first ceiling and yellow stars on blue in the second. Further in it is largely unfinished. The pink granite sarcophagus, shaped like a cartouche, lies in the burial chamber.
story: Siptah came to the throne as a boy after Seti II died. His mummy shows a deformed left foot, perhaps from polio or a club foot, and he died young, perhaps in his mid-teens. Real power lay with Seti's widow, Queen Tausert, and the chancellor Bay until Bay was executed in Siptah's fifth year. The tomb tells the politics: Siptah's cartouches were cut out and later recarved throughout, and one view links the erasures to Tausert and the restorations to his supporters. The burial chamber was never finished, and a side passage was abandoned after the diggers broke into an earlier queen's tomb, KV32. Edward Ayrton found the entrance for Theodore Davis on 18 December 1905. The king's mummy had long since been moved to the cache in Amenhotep II's tomb.
details: First corridor ceiling: vultures with outstretched wings, guarding the way in.
Second corridor ceiling: yellow stars on dark blue.
Cartouches near the entrance: look for signs of recutting where Siptah's name was erased and restored.
The sarcophagus lid: the king as Osiris between Isis and Nephthys.
fun_fact: When the sarcophagus was cleared, all it held was a handful of bones from someone buried centuries after Siptah.
narration: A boy king with a deformed foot was buried here: Siptah. His mummy shows the left foot twisted, perhaps by polio, and he died young, maybe in his mid-teens. He was a king in name only. The real power lay with the old king's widow, Queen Tausert, and a chancellor called Bay, probably of Syrian origin, until Bay was executed. Even Siptah's name became a political football: his cartouches here were cut out and later carved back in. The beginning of the tomb is lovely, with the Litany of Ra on the walls and vultures spreading their wings across the ceiling. Then the work stops. Look up at those vultures in the first corridor, guarding the boy on his way in.

summary: A burial chamber frozen mid-job: red grids, black corrections, carving and paint side by side show exactly how a royal tomb was made.
look: A jogged-axis tomb: stairs and corridors to a well shaft, a pillared hall, then steps down to the burial chamber with the red granite sarcophagus. Decoration starts at the well: painted raised relief on a blue-grey ground. In the burial chamber the walls stand at every stage of work, from red grid lines to finished paint. Often closed.
story:
Horemheb was a general who served Tutankhamun and Ay and then became king himself. He completed the return to the old order after Akhenaten's revolution, and later had his predecessors left off the official king lists. As a general he had already built a fine tomb at Saqqara; as king he started again here.

Edward Ayrton found the tomb for Theodore Davis in February 1908. It marks a turning point: the first royal tomb with painted raised relief instead of plain painting, the figures standing out from a blue-grey ground, and the first to put the Book of Gates in the burial chamber instead of the Amduat.

It was never finished, which is its gift to us. On the burial chamber walls you can follow every stage: a red grid laid down, figures sketched, corrected in black, then cut into relief, then painted. The red granite sarcophagus, shaped like a shrine, has a protective goddess at each corner.

Ayrton found the tomb robbed, with bones of several people. Some think Horemheb is among them. Graffiti from the end of the New Kingdom, one naming Herihor, suggest the priests checked on the burial.
details: Burial chamber walls: red grid squares and red sketches, with black corrections by a senior artist.
Next to them: the same kind of figures cut into relief, some painted, some bare stone.
Well room and antechamber: Horemheb offering to the gods, in raised relief on blue-grey.
The red granite sarcophagus: a goddess with outstretched wings at each corner.
fun_fact: Horemheb's first tomb, at Saqqara, was built while he was still a general. After he became king, a royal cobra was added to his brow on its reliefs.
narration: Horemheb, whose tomb this is, was the general who became king after Tutankhamun and Ay. He finished restoring the old gods after Akhenaten's revolution, and later had his predecessors left off the official lists of kings. As a general he had already built himself a fine tomb at Saqqara; as king he started again here. This tomb marks a change of style. It was the first royal tomb carved in raised relief and then painted, with bright figures standing out from a blue-grey background, and the first to put the Book of Gates in the burial chamber. But the best thing about it is that it was never finished. On the burial chamber walls, work stopped at every stage at once. In one place you see the red grid of squares the draughtsmen laid down. Next to it, figures sketched in red, then corrected in black by a senior hand. Then figures half cut into the stone, and finally some fully painted. It is a workshop frozen in time. Find a red grid and follow it along the wall until the figures become carved and coloured.

summary: Once used as a rubbish dump, it turned out to be the largest tomb in the valley: a family vault for the sons of Ramesses II.
look: You cannot go in. The entrance is a modest doorway low on the valley floor, opposite Ramesses II's own tomb, KV7, and not far from Tutankhamun's. Behind it, corridors run deep into the hill, with at least 130 rooms known so far.
story:
James Burton poked into this tomb in 1825, and in 1902 Howard Carter used its entrance as a dump for his spoil. It looked like a small, ruined, flood-filled tomb. Kent Weeks of the Theban Mapping Project began clearing it in 1987, and in 1995 he crawled through the debris of a pillared hall, 16 pillars strong, and found corridors leading on and on. It was the most dramatic find in the valley since Tutankhamun.

At least 130 rooms were known by 2006, laid out along long corridors, with a large statue of Osiris among the finds. Ramesses II reigned 66 years and fathered dozens of children; many died before him, and this seems to have been their family vault. Skull fragments of his eldest son, Amunherkhepeshef, were found and reconstructed. The other finds are humble but telling: thousands of potsherds, shabtis, beads, ostraca and glass vials.

Robbers emptied it in antiquity and flash floods packed it with debris. By 2006 only about 7 percent of the rooms had been cleared. The work is slow, careful and continuing, and the tomb is closed to visitors.
details: The entrance: a modest doorway low on the valley floor, easy to walk past.
Across the path: KV7, Ramesses II's own tomb. Father and sons lie a stone's throw apart.
The low level of the doorway: flood debris from the slopes above poured straight in.
The path you are on: Carter dumped his rubble here in 1902 without suspecting anything.
fun_fact: In 2006 Weeks's team reckoned only about 7 percent of the rooms had been cleared. Archaeology here runs on geological time.
narration: In front of you is the tomb known as K V 5, the tomb of the sons of Ramesses the Second. You cannot go in, but it is worth a minute. For most of two centuries nobody thought much of it. An explorer looked in in 1825, and in 1902 Howard Carter dumped his rubble at its door. Then, in 1995, the American Egyptologist Kent Weeks, who had been clearing it for years, crawled through the debris of a pillared hall and found corridors running on and on into the hill. It is now the largest tomb in the valley, with at least 130 rooms. Ramesses the Second reigned for 66 years and had dozens of children. Many of his sons died before him, and this seems to have been their family vault. Fragments of the skull of his eldest son were found inside, along with thousands of potsherds, beads and little funerary figures. Robbers emptied it long ago and floods packed it with rubble, so the clearing is slow and still going on. Turn around and look across the path: that is Ramesses' own tomb, so father and sons lie a stone's throw apart.

period: New Kingdom, late 18th Dynasty, c. 1330 BC
summary: A small chamber held a coffin with its gold face ripped off and its names cut out; the bones inside may be Akhenaten, Tutankhamun's father.
look: A small, undecorated tomb, 27.6 metres long: 20 steps down, a corridor and a single chamber. It is closed, so this is a story stop. The entrance is cut into the bedrock of the valley floor, just below Ramesses IX's tomb, KV6.
story:
On 6 January 1907 Edward Ayrton, digging for Theodore Davis, uncovered a staircase here, and three days later they went in. The little chamber held a jumble from Akhenaten's court: panels of a gilded shrine made by Akhenaten for his mother, Queen Tiye; four alabaster canopic jars whose stoppers probably show Kiya, one of his wives; magic bricks naming Akhenaten; and a coffin, most likely made for Kiya, whose names had been cut out and whose gold face had been torn away. Davis announced he had found Queen Tiye. But the bones were a man's.

Who is he? Age estimates have swung for a century, from about 20 to 35-45 in CT scans published in 2010 and 2016. A DNA study published in 2010 found that this man was a son of Amenhotep III and the father of Tutankhamun, which fits Akhenaten. Others prefer the shadowy king Smenkhkare, an idea going back to 1931, and the genetic arguments continue.

Most Egyptologists think the burial was brought here from Amarna after the court abandoned the city, then partly dismantled later. The coffin was long displayed in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo.
details: The entrance: cut into the bedrock of the valley floor, which was lower in Tutankhamun's day.
Twenty steps down to one undecorated chamber; nothing remains inside.
Look up to KV6 and across towards KV62: the Amarna family story lies within a few minutes' walk.
fun_fact: Davis published his find as The Tomb of Queen Tiyi. The real Tiye was found a few hundred metres away, in KV35, and the skeleton here was a man.
narration: Below Ramesses the Ninth's tomb is a small closed doorway, K V 55, and it hides one of the great mysteries of Egyptology. In January 1907 Edward Ayrton, digging for the American Theodore Davis, went down 20 steps into a single bare room. Inside was a jumble from Akhenaten's court: panels of a gilded shrine he made for his mother, Queen Tiye, canopic jars with a woman's face, magic bricks naming Akhenaten, and a beautiful coffin. Someone had cut the names off the coffin and torn away its gold face, as if to erase whoever lay inside. Davis announced that he had found Queen Tiye. But the bones were a man's. In 2010 a DNA study found that he was a son of Amenhotep the Third and the father of Tutankhamun, which points to Akhenaten himself, though some still prefer a shadowy king called Smenkhkare. So, possibly, the heretic king who tried to replace the gods was buried here without a name. Look at the entrance, cut into the valley floor itself, and imagine the priests carrying him down.

summary: The first tomb by the entrance road and often empty of people: short, straight, with the king's grave sealed by an upside-down stone box.
look: A single straight corridor leads to the burial chamber and a small unfinished end room. In the chamber, the burial pit is covered by a stone box turned upside down, roughly cartouche-shaped. Nut stretches twice across the ceiling; Greek graffiti mark the corridor.
story: Ramesses VII died in his seventh year, and his workmen made do. They widened a corridor into a burial chamber and abandoned the room beyond. The decoration follows the tomb of Ramesses VI closely: the Book of Gates, the Book of Caverns and the Book of the Earth, with a double Nut on the burial chamber ceiling. Instead of a free-standing sarcophagus, the king lay in a pit in the floor under an upturned stone box, the last known sarcophagus in a royal tomb in the valley. The mummy is lost, though four cups with his name turned up in the Deir el-Bahari cache. Open since antiquity, the tomb carries 132 Greek and Roman graffiti, and Coptic monks later lived here.
details: The stone box over the burial pit: turned upside down, roughly cartouche-shaped.
Burial chamber ceiling: the sky goddess Nut twice, back to back.
Corridor walls: Greek and Roman names scratched by ancient tourists.
The unfinished end room: work stopped when the king died.
fun_fact: In 1743 the traveller Richard Pococke labelled this simply 'Tomb A': it has been first in line for visitors for 2,000 years.
narration: The first tomb you meet on the road in, and often the quietest, belongs to Ramesses the Seventh. He died in his seventh year, so his workmen made do. They widened a corridor into a burial chamber and abandoned the little room beyond. Instead of a standing sarcophagus, the king was laid in a pit in the floor, under an upside-down stone box. The walls copy the tomb of Ramesses the Sixth, with gods of the night and the earth, and the sky goddess Nut stretched twice across the ceiling. Greek and Roman tourists came here too and left 132 graffiti. Look for their scratched names in the corridor as you walk in.

summary: The tomb of Egypt's most famous king is one of the most ruined in the valley, packed by floods with debris that set like concrete.
look: Closed. The entrance is low on the valley floor, opposite KV5 and near Merenptah's tomb, KV8. Inside, a corridor descends about 58 metres before the axis bends towards the burial chamber; most of the decoration is lost.
story: Ramesses II started this tomb before the end of his second year, and the work took 10 to 12 years. The builders cut it low in the valley floor. Flash floods have filled it again and again with debris that hardened like cement, destroying most of the decoration. Christian Leblanc's Franco-Egyptian mission has been clearing and conserving it since 1991. In a recess appears Nefertari's cartouche: the only queen shown in her husband's tomb in the Ramesside period. Ramesses' mummy was moved by priests to his father Seti I's tomb, then to the Deir el-Bahari cache; it is now at NMEC. Greek visitors scratched names in the first corridor, among them Echeboulos of Rhodes and a man from Cyprus.
details: The entrance, low on the valley floor: compare it with tombs cut into the cliffs higher up.
Across the path: KV5, the tomb of his sons.
A few steps away: KV8, the tomb of his son and successor Merenptah.
fun_fact: The great king's granite sarcophagus was reused around 1000 BC by a high priest of Amun, Menkheperre.
narration: In front of you, low on the valley floor, is the tomb of Ramesses the Second, Egypt's most famous king, and one of the most ruined tombs in the valley. The builders cut it too low. For three thousand years flash floods have poured in, filling it with mud and stones that set almost like cement. Most of the paintings are gone. A French team led by Christian Leblanc has been clearing it since 1991. The king himself left long ago: priests moved his mummy to his father's tomb and then to a hidden cache, and today he lies in Cairo. Even ancient Greek tourists came by, one of them from Rhodes. Notice how the entrance sits almost at the level of the path.

period: Middle and New Kingdom, c. 2050-1425 BC; Coptic monastery 6th-8th century AD
summary: A natural amphitheatre of cliffs under the Qurn, where three kings across six centuries built terraced temples facing Karnak.
look: Face the cliffs: Hatshepsut's three terraces are in the middle, the low ruins of Mentuhotep II's temple to the left, and the scant remains of Thutmose III's temple tucked between them, higher up. The bay of cliffs rises behind towards the Qurn. The royal cache tomb is in a hidden recess of the cliffs further south.
story:
The Arabic name, Deir el-Bahari, means 'the Northern Monastery', after the Coptic monastery of Saint Phoibammon that stood on Hatshepsut's upper terrace from the 6th to the 8th century AD; its monks painted over some reliefs. But the bay was holy long before.

Around 2050 BC Mentuhotep II, the Theban king who reunited Egypt, built his temple and tomb here, terraced against the cliff. About five centuries later Hatshepsut placed her temple right next to it, borrowing its terraces and outdoing them. Thutmose III then squeezed a third temple, Djeser-Akhet, between the two, higher up; the Polish-Egyptian mission found it in 1961-62 under rockfall.

Orientation is meaning here. Hatshepsut's temple points across the Nile to Karnak. Each year, in the Beautiful Festival of the Valley, Amun's statue left Karnak in its sacred boat, crossed the river and visited the temples of the west bank, while Theban families feasted at the tombs of their dead.

In a hidden recess of the southern cliffs, priests of the 21st Dynasty hid the royal mummies in tomb DB320, the great cache found in 1881; another cache, Bab el-Gasus, held 153 reburied priests.

The excavators read like a roll call: Mariette, Naville from the 1890s, Herbert Winlock for the Metropolitan Museum in 1911-31, and the Polish mission from 1961. In November 1997 the temple was the scene of a terrorist attack in which more than 60 people died; today security is tight and the site is calm. A small electric train runs from the visitor centre towards the temple, welcome in the heat.
details: Left of Hatshepsut's temple: the low ruined terraces of Mentuhotep II's temple, five centuries older.
Between the two, higher up: the scant remains of Thutmose III's temple, found in 1961-62.
The cliff behind the temple: its vertical folds echo the rows of columns below.
Turn round on any terrace: the temple's axis points across the river to Karnak.
fun_fact: The name means 'Northern Monastery': for the villagers who named it, the memorable thing here was a Christian monastery, not a pharaoh's temple.
narration: In front of you is Deir el-Bahari, a great bay of golden cliffs under the peak of the Qurn, and one of the most sacred places on the west bank. The name is Arabic for the Northern Monastery, because Coptic monks once lived on the top terrace of the temple you see. But the story starts thousands of years before them. Around 2050 BC, King Mentuhotep the Second, who reunited Egypt, built a terraced temple and tomb against these cliffs. Look to the left of the big temple: those low ruins are his. Five centuries later Hatshepsut chose the spot next door, borrowed his idea of terraces, and outdid it. Then Thutmose the Third squeezed a third temple in between them, higher up, now just a scatter of stones. Why here? Turn around and look east. The temples point across the river to Karnak. Once a year, at the Beautiful Festival of the Valley, the statue of Amun left Karnak in his gilded boat and crossed the Nile to visit, while families picnicked at the tombs of their ancestors. And there is a secret in these cliffs: in a hidden shaft to the south, priests hid the mummies of Egypt's greatest kings, found only in 1881. Now look at the cliff behind the temple and notice how its vertical folds echo the rows of columns: the architect designed with the mountain.

summary: A woman who ruled as king built Egypt's most modern-looking temple: three colonnaded terraces set against a cliff, called 'Holy of Holies'.
look: Face the cliff: a long ramp climbs through three terraces, each fronted by a colonnade. On the middle terrace the Punt reliefs are in the colonnade to the left of the ramp and the Divine Birth to the right; the Hathor chapel is at the far left end, the Anubis chapel at the far right. On top, a row of statues of the queen as Osiris fronts the upper court, with the sanctuary cut into the rock behind.
story:
Hatshepsut, daughter of Thutmose I and widow of Thutmose II, ruled first as regent for her young stepson Thutmose III and then, by about his seventh year, as king herself. She called this temple Djeser-djeseru, 'Holy of Holies', built it between her 7th and 20th years, and dedicated it to Amun as 'a garden for my father Amun'. Its architect may have been her steward Senenmut, or the high priest Hapuseneb.

The temple is 273.5 metres long. A causeway about a kilometre long, lined with more than 100 sandstone sphinxes, the oldest known sphinx avenue, led up from the valley temple. Persea trees and T-shaped pools stood on the lower terrace. The axis points across the Nile to Karnak, and around the winter solstice the rising sun shines along it into the sanctuary.

About 20 years after her death, late in Thutmose III's reign, her names and images were hacked out and her statues smashed. Akhenaten's men later erased Amun. Later kings restored, the Ptolemies added chapels for healing gods, and Christians built a monastery on top.

Much of what you see has been rebuilt. The Polish-Egyptian mission has worked here since 1961, reassembling blocks and statues; the upper terrace reopened in 2000, the solar court in 2015 and the Amun sanctuary in 2017.
details: In front of the lower terrace: ancient tree pits and a stump, said to be from the incense trees of Punt.
Middle terrace, left colonnade: the expedition to Punt.
Middle terrace, right colonnade: the divine birth of Hatshepsut.
Upper terrace: the queen as Osiris, arms crossed, wearing a king's false beard.
At the top, turn round: the temple's axis runs straight across the fields to Karnak.
fun_fact: Many of Hatshepsut's statues in museums were pieced together from fragments that Herbert Winlock dug out of dumps near the causeway, which is why New York's Metropolitan Museum has so many.
narration: Before you is the temple of Hatshepsut, the woman who ruled Egypt as king for about 20 years. She called it Djeser Djeseru, the Holy of Holies, and dedicated it to the god Amun as, in her words, a garden for my father. Its clean lines and colonnades look almost modern, and they are set right against the cliff, so that the mountain itself becomes the back wall. Hatshepsut was the daughter of one king and the widow of another. When her husband died, she ruled for her young stepson, Thutmose the Third, and then simply made herself king, with the titles, the crown and even the false beard. The temple, possibly designed by her steward Senenmut, makes her case in stone. Walk up the ramp to the middle terrace. On your left, her ships sail to the land of Punt for incense. On your right, the god Amun himself fathers her. Higher up, the queen stands as Osiris, arms crossed. About 20 years after her death, Thutmose the Third had her name and her face hacked out all over Egypt, here included, and her statues smashed. What you see has been patiently pieced back together by a Polish and Egyptian team working here since 1961. When you reach the top terrace, turn around: the temple's axis runs straight across the river to Karnak, the house of her father Amun.

period: New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, expedition in year 9 of Hatshepsut, c. 1471 BC
summary: A travel report in stone: Hatshepsut's ships sail to the incense land of Punt, meet its king and queen, and bring home live myrrh trees.
look: Middle terrace, in the colonnade to the left (south) of the central ramp. The scenes cover the back wall in registers: Punt itself with its stilt houses, the ships under sail and being loaded, and the cargo presented to Amun and measured. Queen Ati's figure here is a cast; the original block is in Cairo.
story:
In year 9 of her reign, about 1471 BC, Hatshepsut sent five ships down the Red Sea to Punt, the land of incense, under the chancellor Nehsi. Egyptians had traded with Punt since at least the 5th Dynasty, but nobody recorded a voyage like this. Where was Punt? Most scholars place it on the African coast of the southern Red Sea, around Eritrea, Sudan, northern Ethiopia or Somalia. Studies of mummified baboons, whose isotopes and DNA match animals from Eritrea and its region, point the same way.

The reliefs read like a reporter's notebook. The Puntites live in round houses on stilts, reached by ladders, among palms and myrrh trees. Their king, Parahu, comes forward with his wife, Queen Ati, a strikingly large woman whom modern doctors have diagnosed in every way imaginable; nearby is a small donkey, captioned as the one that carries his wife. The Egyptians load myrrh trees in baskets, ebony, ivory, gold, animal skins and baboons. Under the ships swim fish drawn so accurately that Red Sea species can be identified.

Back home the haul is presented to Amun, the incense measured in heaps and the gold weighed. The texts say 31 live myrrh trees came back, to be planted in Amun's garden here, which is why this is often called the first recorded plant-collecting expedition.

The original Queen Ati block went to Cairo in the 19th century; what you see is a cast. You may find the original at the Grand Egyptian Museum or still at the Tahrir museum; trust the label.
details: The village of Punt: round houses on stilts with ladders, under palms and trees.
Queen Ati, large and heavy-set, walking behind her slim husband, King Parahu.
Myrrh trees with their root balls in baskets, carried on poles up to the ships.
Under the ships: Red Sea fish and a turtle, drawn precisely enough to name the species.
Baboons on board among the cargo, bound for Thebes.
fun_fact: Some of the frankincense was charred and ground into kohl eyeliner: the first recorded use of the resin that way.
narration: You are standing in front of the Punt colonnade, the record of Hatshepsut's great trading expedition. In her ninth year, around 1471 BC, five ships sailed down the Red Sea to Punt, the land of incense. Most scholars now place Punt on the African coast, around Eritrea, and studies of mummified baboons brought back from there point the same way. The carvers recorded the trip like reporters. Look for the people of Punt living in round houses on stilts, reached by ladders, under palm trees. Their king comes to meet the Egyptians, followed by his wife, Queen Ati, a very large woman, and a little donkey whose caption says it is the animal that carries her. The Egyptians load their ships with ebony, ivory, gold, animal skins and baboons. Most precious of all are the myrrh trees, dug up with their roots and carried aboard in baskets slung from poles. The texts say 31 live trees came home, to be planted in Amun's garden right here. Under the ships, the sea is full of fish, drawn so accurately that experts can name the Red Sea species. One warning: the Queen Ati you see is a cast, and the original block is in a Cairo museum. Now find the myrrh trees in their baskets, and follow them up the gangplank.
